title: Stacking Legal Skills: How Stints at Big Law, Biz Dev and and Legal Ops Paved the Way to the C-Suite for Akshay Verma (COO, SpotDraft)
author: Akshay Verma

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source argues that lawyers must develop practical AI skills and describes an agentic knowledge-management initiative, but it does not address whether automation removes formative junior work, creates a verification-expertise paradox, or requires reconstructed apprenticeship through simulation and mentorship.
qs: But if you do not learn AI and how to prompt and how to leverage it as a lawyer, yeah, you're going to be outdated.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: Verma accepts the lawyer-guided framing and materially extends it by identifying policy and procedure retrieval as a concrete legal-department knowledge-management problem motivating an agentic product. His account also reinforces the synthesis’s evidentiary caution: Sidebar has about 30 beta customers, but no effectiveness results are supplied.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Verma accepts the cluster’s core view that AI will reallocate tasks rather than replace lawyers wholesale, and materially extends it with a process-led implementation approach: repair contracting workflows first, deploy tools selectively where complexity warrants them, and retain capable human talent to direct adoption.
qs: What it is going to replace are the tasks that lawyers are doing that are not lawyering.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Verma supports bounded agentic deployment in legal departments through internal-system knowledge and contract retrieval, while retaining human source checking and acknowledging stale-data risk. His beta account and projected time savings align with the cluster’s emphasis on orchestration, verification and limited deployment evidence, but do not establish multistep autonomy or broad reliability.
qs: So imagine an agent that's plugged into your systems, it's fully within your firewalls that you can ask a natural question to.
And then it cites its sources, like make sure or confirm this by looking in these documents.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that useful agentic legal AI must connect to organisational context and workflow needs rather than operate as isolated text generation. Verma grounds SpotDraft’s agentic direction in legal-department information-sharing and policy-access problems, while reporting only a beta deployment and no effectiveness results; it does not materially establish how tacit expertise is transferred or quality is verified.
qs: There are a number of pain points that I saw in my time at Facebook and at Coinbase with respect to how information is shared across legal departments.
We've got about 30 customers in beta for a product called Sidebar, which I'm particularly excited about.

st.t: Contract intelligence: Business coordination exceeds document storage
st.an: Verma supports the proposition that contract technology should extend beyond storage or isolated document analysis. He frames CLM as an end-to-end, routinely used enterprise workflow connecting legal, sales, finance and revenue operations, while making contract information accessible after signature. His categorical preference for CLM is one position within the cluster’s separate debate over incumbent products and labels.
qs: This is a tool that the entire company in some fashion touches regularly on a daily basis.
Then we've got other potential teams like finance or rev ops who need the data out of their contracts or the data out of the actual deal.

st.t: Legal leadership: Business capability complements legal expertise
st.an: Verma’s first-person career account supports the proposition that legal leadership benefits from operational and business capability alongside legal training. His Axiom business-development experience exposed him to how corporate legal departments operate and preceded a move into legal operations; his observation of legal operations’ growing prominence further aligns with the cluster. The evidence is experiential, not a universal career formula or systematic industry finding.
qs: That's where I learned the ins and outs of running legal departments.
Then there was this really quick and big shift where the legal ops function and the legal ops role really started becoming prominent, especially in the bigger law departments.

st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: Verma supports the cluster’s account of pragmatic, customer-focused adoption: he links product prospects to product quality and knowledge of customer pain points, while relying on personal experience rather than quantified sales, productivity or customer-outcome evidence.
qs: And if this is the way that we solve people's problems, I know what those pain points are.
And that's exactly what's unfolded over the last two years that I've been there.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Verma supports the cluster’s core view that AI will change lawyers’ work and required skills rather than replace lawyers wholesale. Sidebar’s limited beta also illustrates early, buyer-side deployment focused on a bounded legal-department knowledge-management problem, not proven autonomous legal delivery or broad service-model disruption.
qs: It's this thing that lawyers are not going to be replaced by AI.
We've got about 30 customers in beta for a product called Sidebar, which I'm particularly excited about.

kp.k: Legal operations combines commercial persuasion with spending discipline
kp.d: Verma describes a shift in his Axiom client relationships from predominantly GCs and deputies in 2012–2015 toward increasingly prominent legal operations functions, especially in larger departments. He says Facebook recruited him in 2018 initially to address external legal spending, drawing on his understanding of law firm economics. His account treats business development skills—evangelism, resilience and securing organizational support—as central to operational change, rather than suggesting that legal expertise alone suffices.
qs: That was 2012 to maybe 2015. Then there was this really quick and big shift where the legal ops function and the legal ops role really started becoming prominent, especially in the bigger law departments.
I was brought in initially as my remit was there to address that spend and figure out a way to reduce it.

You're not getting an entire legal department behind an idea, right? You're not doing that. That's not a lawyer thing to do. It's a very business minded thing to do. And it's a critical component of legal operations.

kp.k: Cross-functional experience can support legal professionals entering executive roles
kp.d: Verma presents his transition to SpotDraft COO as an application of accumulated legal practice, business development, operational and technology-buying experience. This is a personal account of a career pathway beyond practicing law or leading legal operations, not evidence of a general AI-driven employment trend.
qs: You've been a lawyer, you've done business development, you understand how sales works, you understand operational efficiency, you understand legal technology, you have bought it, you have evaluated it, you have implemented it, you have ripped it out, you've done all of those things.
This is like the perfect role for you. And like these kinds of roles don't come along very often.

kp.k: Contract management must connect execution with post-signature intelligence
kp.d: Verma argues that businesses struggle both to execute contracts quickly and to understand their contents afterward. He positions SpotDraft, a software vendor selling mostly to legal departments, as an end-to-end CLM product connecting contract requests and signatures with repository data, renewals and terminations. These are vendor claims about product scope and buyer needs, with an explicit qualification that SpotDraft is not suitable for everyone.
qs: And then once they're signed, very few companies actually know what's in their contracts because there's so much rich data that's in their agreements.
But what about what's in my contracts that actually informs what I should be doing in getting my contracts to signature.
So we're not right for everyone.
We missed all these renewal dates. We had these terminations and we actually didn't know about them.

kp.k: Legal technology infrastructure spans contracts, spending and workflows
kp.d: Verma recommends a CLM tool for every legal department, a spend-management tool after $5 million of external spending, and a workflow tool, potentially agentic, for knowledge management, intake and connections to other systems. He qualifies the spending threshold by matter volume and diversity of law firm relationships: one $5 million matter is different from dispersed spending. He also emphasizes that CLM implementation affects sales, legal, finance and revenue operations, not just lawyers.
qs: I say after $5 million of external spend, you need a spend management tool.
I would want to take a look at the volume of matters to really make the call
3 is a workflow tool. This is newer, particularly in the age of AI. Some type of agentic tool that will help you with workflows.
This is a tool that the entire company in some fashion touches regularly on a daily basis.

kp.k: Contracting inefficiency often precedes technology selection
kp.d: Verma identifies three recurring problems: missing centralized repositories, unnecessary review and negotiation of routine NDAs, and absent templates or defined routing and approval processes. He recommends standard terms and self-service signing for ordinary NDAs, retaining negotiation for situations such as joint ventures or highly confidential arrangements. He describes these diagnoses as grounded in data and experience and references Lucy Basili's market survey, but supplies no survey figures, sample details or measured NDA litigation incidence.
qs: And this is a product of data and experience. This is not like Akshay's view on what the problems are.
Number one, number one, most companies don't even have all their contracts in one place.
Put it on a portal, put good terms in there, make people sign it.
Unless it's like we're going into a joint venture, or it's highly confidential, I get that. You'll negotiate that.
I don't have templates for my basic agreements. I don't have a good process for where the contract goes once the business says I need a contract.

kp.k: Software cannot substitute for process and change management
kp.d: Verma argues that vendors are sometimes blamed for failures caused by weak processes or non-adherence inside legal departments. He characterizes lawyers as resistant both to change and its perceived risk, recommending education, preparation and internal evangelism. In his delivery account, documented processes and measured adoption simplify migration; missing processes make platform implementation hazardous. SpotDraft onboarding can take 30, 40 days to maybe 120 days depending on complexity and volume, and customers must establish an approval matrix before going live. He says few customers accept recommended upfront consulting because it adds time and cost.
qs: technology providers get blamed when the real problem is actually lack of process or lack of adherence to process internally in a legal department.
Evangelizing has a lot to do with education and preparation.

Depending on the customer, their complexity, it can be 30, 40 days. It can be up to maybe 120 days, just depending on what needs to be done for the customer and how complex and voluminous their onboarding is.
That is where a lack of process or bad process put into a SpotDraft platform is a recipe for disaster.
Very few customers take us up on that. A, it's more money, it's more time.
You cannot set up in a SpotDraft platform without having an approval matrix.

kp.k: AI substitutes non-lawyering tasks rather than lawyers, Verma predicts
kp.d: Verma rejects the reported expectation that AI will replace all lawyers. His own prediction is that AI will replace non-lawyering tasks, especially within in-house departments, while changing departmental structure, size and work. He supplies no quantified staffing projection or empirical displacement evidence and maintains that lawyering itself will not change.
qs: No, it's not. It's not going to replace lawyers. What it is going to replace are the tasks that lawyers are doing that are not lawyering.
And there's so much of that that goes on in house.
So will it change the structure, the size, the nature of legal departments? Absolutely. But it's not going to change lawyering.

kp.k: Human talent and AI literacy remain essential
kp.d: Verma argues that people remain necessary to develop, adopt and evolve technology, even as required skills change rapidly. He endorses learning prompting and practical AI use as a condition of remaining professionally current, comparing refusal to learn AI with a contemporary lawyer refusing email. This is a skills recommendation and historical analogy, not a measured finding about employment outcomes.
qs: You have to find the right talent to make sure that the technology is developed properly, is adopted properly, and that it evolves properly.
The nature of what that talent needs to be able to do is changing very, very quickly.
But if you do not learn AI and how to prompt and how to leverage it as a lawyer, yeah, you're going to be outdated.
Could you imagine a lawyer today be like, yeah, I don't use email. I don't use email. How are you going to communicate?

kp.k: Sidebar targets internal knowledge retrieval and contract questions
kp.d: Verma reports about 30 customers in beta for Sidebar, which he calls SpotDraft's agentic offering. He describes natural-language access to internal policies, procedures and contract repository data, with answers and source citations within company firewalls. The examples concern retrieval and answering rather than demonstrated autonomous multi-step execution. His projected time savings are illustrative, not measured beta results; he explicitly notes that underlying documents may be outdated and describes checking cited documents.
qs: We've got about 30 customers in beta for a product called Sidebar, which I'm particularly excited about. And that's our agentic play.
So imagine an agent that's plugged into your systems, it's fully within your firewalls that you can ask a natural question to.
And then it cites its sources, like make sure or confirm this by looking in these documents. Maybe those documents are updated, maybe they're not.
But the point is you've saved yourself an hour, two hours, three hours, maybe a couple of days
Being able to ask your contract repository, natural language questions that give you the information and data that you need at your fingertips very, very quickly.

kp.k: SpotDraft envisions a broader legal operations platform
kp.d: Verma frames agentic knowledge and contract-data capabilities as part of an intended operating system for legal operations teams and departments. He connects this direction to a revised company mission and to legal operations' longstanding effort to change how legal work is performed. This is a vendor strategy and future vision, not evidence that the wider market has already adopted such an operating model.
qs: So I think those kinds of agentic plays have a huge role in what I will call the operating system for legal ops teams and for the legal department.
And that's the direction that we're headed.
Our new mission statement is building the future of how legal works.
By the way, this is a drum that the legal ops profession has been beating since inception.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Akshay Verma predicts that AI will replace non-lawyering tasks rather than lawyers or lawyering, while changing legal departments' structure, size and work.
pts.d: Verma explicitly rejects wholesale lawyer replacement. His task-substitution claim focuses on the substantial amount of non-lawyering work performed in-house. He predicts organisational change but does not specify whether departments will become larger or smaller, identify a staffing shape, or quantify job losses.

pts.k: Verma argues that AI changes required lawyer capabilities and that lawyers who do not learn to use it risk becoming outdated.
pts.d: Verma endorses the need to learn AI, prompting and practical use in legal work. He treats this as a continuation of earlier technology-driven changes, using email adoption as an analogy. This is a claim about professional adaptation rather than a demonstrated employment outcome. He also maintains that human talent remains necessary to develop, adopt and evolve technology.

pts.k: Verma claims that agentic workflow tools can help legal departments organise knowledge, connect contracting workflows and handle business intake.
pts.d: He presents an agentic or workflow tool as the third component of his recommended legal-technology toolkit, alongside CLM and spend management. Proposed uses include knowledge management, workflows connected to CLM and a channel through which business colleagues engage legal. The source calls these tools agentic but does not describe autonomous legal decision-making or detailed multi-step execution.

pts.k: Verma predicts that internal knowledge and contract-query agents can sharply reduce information-search time and become part of an operating system for legal departments.
pts.d: Discussing SpotDraft's Sidebar beta, Verma describes natural-language access to company policies and procedures, with answers and source citations, and natural-language queries of a contract repository. He suggests these capabilities could save hours or occasionally days otherwise spent searching or waiting for colleagues. These are illustrative benefits, not reported measured savings. His example retains human confirmation through cited documents rather than describing reliance on autonomous legal advice.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The AI claims rest primarily on Verma's operational experience, technology-adoption analogies and descriptions of a vendor beta, rather than measured AI outcomes.
pts.d: Verma draws on his legal operations roles at Facebook and Coinbase to identify information-sharing problems and on his wider career to argue for continued human involvement. He speaks as SpotDraft's COO about the company's product direction. The approximately 30 beta customers establish reported testing activity, not demonstrated effectiveness. No AI benchmarks, controlled comparisons, measured productivity results or employment data are supplied. His separate reference to survey data concerns contract-management practices, not evidence that AI achieves the predicted changes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Verma describes current experimentation and rapidly changing skills, with no fixed deadline for broader organisational transformation.
pts.d: In the supplied 2026-labelled source, Verma says the company is focused on agents now and Sidebar is in beta; he gives no general-release date. His predictions about legal department structure and lawyer adaptation have no specified horizon. The knowledge-search scenario assumes connection to internal systems within company firewalls, and he acknowledges that retrieved documents may be outdated. His broader technology-implementation discussion makes sound processes, adoption work and human talent conditions for successful deployment; it is not an AI-specific outcome study.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are corporate legal departments, in-house lawyers, legal operations professionals and business colleagues seeking legal information or support.
pts.d: In-house lawyers would have non-lawyering tasks substituted and need AI-use skills; legal leaders would face changes to department organisation and talent requirements. Legal operations teams would use workflow and knowledge tools to organise service delivery. Legal staff and business users could obtain internal policies and contract information more quickly. SpotDraft is presented as a B2B software vendor selling primarily to legal departments, not an ALSP delivering legal work. The source makes no concrete AI prediction about access to justice, law-firm billing or public legal services.
